seeds.scene: A chess board mid-game shown from White's side. White pieces: King e1, Queen d1, Rook a1, Rook h1, Bishop c4, Knight f3, Pawns a2, b2, c3, d4, e4, f2, g2, h2. Recompute: pieces of Black currently giving check or attacking white pieces — Bishop c5 attacks pawn on f2 (diagonal c5-d4(white pawn)-e3-f2 blocked by white d4). So Bc5 attacks d4. Nf6 attacks e4 (knight move). Pawn e5 attacks d4 and f4 — d4 is white, f4 is empty. So attacks: Bc5→d4, Nf6→e4, Pe5→d4. Three attacking pieces.
seeds.question: How many of Black's pieces are currently attacking a White piece?
seeds.lever: Read board state precisely (square by square) and apply chess movement rules including blocked diagonals; count attacker-pieces (not attacks).

But sliding diagonally with 30cm thickness: 30×175 = leaves 198×30 cross-section → 198 fits in 200 width? Yes. Push mattress diagonally tilted through 200 wide door, since 30 thick fits height-wise. Verify: standing mattress on edge (203 vertical) — door height only 175, so 203 won't fit upright. Tilt 30°: mattress projection at angle... Check: at angle θ, projected diagonal = 203·cosθ + 30·sinθ ≤ 175 (height) and 198·cosθ + 30·sinθ ≤ 200 (width). At θ=30°, 203·0.866+30·0.5=175.8+15=190.8 > 175. Need θ larger. At θ=45°: 203·0.707+30·0.707=164.7 ≤ 175 ✓; width 198·0.707+30·0.707=161 ≤ 200 ✓. So yes, fits diagonally.

seeds.scene: A cliff edge 10 m high with a person throwing a ball horizontally outward at moderate speed. A grid of 1m squares is overlaid for reference. seeds.answer: Bucket B
seeds.lever: Compute time to fall: t = √(2h/g) = √(20/9.8) ≈ 1.43 s. Horizontal distance = 5 × 1.43 ≈ 7.14 m → bucket B (at 7m).

seeds.scene: A tall transparent jar holds three immiscible liquids in clear stratified layers (top to bottom): vegetable oil, water, honey. seeds.answer: cork, wax, plastic bead, grape, steel marble

seeds.scene: A side view of a wrench applied to a hex bolt. Three force-arrows are drawn at different positions along the wrench handle: F1 at 5 cm from the bolt, magnitude 50 N. F2 at 15 cm, magnitude 30 N. F3 at 25 cm, magnitude 15 N. All three forces are perpendicular to the handle.

seeds.scene: Two ceramic cups sitting on a cool kitchen counter (room temp 20°C). Cup A held boiling water (98°C) and has been sitting for 30 minutes. Cup B held cold water (5°C) and has also been sitting for 30 minutes. The room is well-ventilated.

seeds.scene: A Newton's cradle with 5 identical steel balls. The leftmost 2 balls are pulled back together and released. Question: predict what happens at the right side.

seeds.lever: Conservation of momentum + energy in equal-mass elastic collision; n balls in → n balls out.

seeds.scene: A diagram of a single-block-and-tackle pulley system: a fixed pulley at the top, a movable pulley supporting a 100 kg load, with one end of the rope attached to the ceiling and the other end pulled down by a person. Two segments of rope support the movable pulley.

seeds.answer: Half the load weight ≈ 500 N (or 50 kg-force)
seeds.lever: Pulley mechanical advantage = number of supporting rope segments (2); force = weight / 2.

seeds.scene: Three identical 100mL water spills on the floor of three different rooms. Room A: warm (28°C), low humidity (30%), windy fan blowing. Room B: cool (18°C), high humidity (80%), still air. Room C: warm (28°C), high humidity (80%), still air. Surface area of each spill is the same.
seeds.question: Which spill EVAPORATES FASTEST?
seeds.answer: Room A
seeds.lever: Evaporation favored by high temp + low humidity + airflow; A wins on all three.

seeds.scene: A ramp with adjustable angle. A crate sits on the ramp. The coefficient of static friction is μ=0.3 (printed on the ramp). The ramp angle indicator reads 20°.
seeds.question: Will the crate slide?
seeds.answer: Yes
seeds.lever: Compare tan(angle) with μ_s; tan 20° ≈ 0.364 > μ = 0.3, so static friction is exceeded → crate slides.

seeds.scene: Three bar magnets laid out on a table with their N (red) and S (blue) poles labeled. Magnet 1: N-left, S-right. Magnet 2: S-left, N-right. Magnet 3: N-left, S-right. Each pair shown side by side with a small gap. Pair (1,2) faces N-S, Pair (2,3) faces N-N, Pair (1,3) faces S-N.
seeds.question: Which pairs ATTRACT each other?
seeds.answer: Only pair (1,3)
seeds.lever: Determine the facing-pole pair for each adjacency. Pair (1,2): S of 1 meets S of 2 → repel. Pair (2,3): N of 2 meets N of 3 → repel. Pair (1,3): S of 1 meets N of 3 → attract.

seeds.scene: A ramp with two objects placed at the top: a solid metal cylinder (free to roll) and a flat metal block (sliding only). Both have the same mass. The ramp has very low friction (effectively frictionless for sliding). They are released simultaneously.

seeds.answer: The sliding block
seeds.lever: Rolling cylinder has rotational kinetic energy + translational; sliding block has only translational → all PE → translational KE → faster (assuming low friction).

seeds.scene: Three identical light bulbs labeled A, B, C arranged in a circuit: bulb A is in series with the parallel combination of B and C. The circuit is powered by a 9V battery.
seeds.question: Which bulb is the BRIGHTEST?
seeds.answer: Bulb A
seeds.lever: Bulb A carries the full current; bulbs B and C share current (each gets half). Brightness scales with power = I²R; A has higher current.

seeds.scene: A row of 8 standing dominos. Domino 1 is leaning toward domino 2 by ~3°, the others are perfectly upright. Spacing between adjacent dominos is 4 cm; each domino is 5 cm tall and 2 cm wide. Domino 1 is given a slight push toward domino 2.

seeds.scene: Top-down view of a ripple tank with two point wave sources S1 and S2 separated by 6 cm, oscillating in phase. Wavelength is 2 cm. A detector point P sits at distance 7 cm from S1 and 5 cm from S2.

seeds.answer: Constructive
seeds.lever: Path difference = 7-5 = 2 cm = 1λ → integer multiple of wavelength → constructive.

seeds.scene: A railway track has a 6 mm gap between two rail segments at 10°C ambient temperature. The rail is steel (linear expansion coefficient α = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ /°C). One rail segment is 25 m long. Summer can reach 40°C.
seeds.question: By how much will one rail segment expand by summer? Will the gap close?
seeds.answer: Expansion ≈ 9 mm; gap will close (and rails would press)
seeds.lever: ΔL = α × L × ΔT = 1.2e-5 × 25000 mm × 30°C = 9 mm; 9 mm > 6 mm gap → closes.

seeds.scene: A balance beam pivoted at center. Left side: a 2 kg weight at 30 cm from pivot, AND a 1 kg weight at 50 cm from pivot. Right side: a 4 kg weight at unknown distance d.

seeds.lever: Sum left moments: 2×30 + 1×50 = 110 kg·cm. Set equal to right: 4 × d = 110 → d = 27.5 cm.

seeds.scene: A tall water tank 5 m deep, with a small valve at the bottom. Pressure gauge at depth 2 m reads 20 kPa above atmospheric. Tank is open to air.

seeds.lever: Pressure scales linearly with depth; 20 kPa at 2 m → 10 kPa per meter; at 5 m → 50 kPa.

seeds.lever: Conservation of angular momentum L = Iω; reducing I (arms in) increases ω.

seeds.scene: A row of 5 dominos stands upright. Each domino is 5 cm tall, 2 cm wide. Spacing between consecutive dominos increases linearly: 3, 5, 7, 9 cm gaps. Domino 1 is pushed.

From BELOW (looking up at the table from underneath, transparent table), the same 5 objects are seen from underneath; the mug shows its bottom (round circular base), the book shows its back cover (red), the plate shows its underside, the phone shows its back, the pen looks the same.
seeds.question: Which object's top view is most DIFFERENT from its bottom view?
seeds.answer: The mug (top shows opening with handle, bottom shows flat circular base)
seeds.lever: Reason about object asymmetry top-vs-bottom; mug is most asymmetric.

seeds.scene: A construction site shown in 4 panels: aerial, front, left, right views. From aerial: 6 cranes visible. Front view: 4 cranes lined up. Left view: 3 cranes. Right view: 4 cranes. Some cranes overlap from each ground angle.
seeds.question: What is the TRUE number of cranes (using aerial as authoritative)?
seeds.lever: Aerial view gives unobstructed count; ground views suffer from occlusion.

seeds.scene: A selfie taken in a bathroom mirror. The person wears a wristwatch on their LEFT wrist (in real life). In the mirrored selfie, the watch APPEARS to be on the person's RIGHT wrist (because mirrors flip).
seeds.question: Which wrist is the watch ACTUALLY on?
seeds.answer: Left wrist
seeds.lever: Reverse mirror flip: image of right wrist = actual left.

seeds.scene: A photo of 4 trees A, B, C, D. Tree A's silhouette is partially behind C. C's silhouette is partially behind D. D's silhouette is fully visible (in front of all). B is fully visible (no overlap with others).
seeds.question: Which tree is FARTHEST from the camera?
seeds.answer: Tree A
seeds.lever: Occlusion ordering: D in front, C behind D, A behind C → A farthest. B's depth indeterminate.

seeds.scene: A box with the logo 'BOX' printed clearly on the front. Three views: front (logo readable as 'BOX'), back (no logo), top (no logo). A reflected view in a mirror behind the box shows the back of the box (no logo) with 'XOB' visible (mirrored 'BOX' from the front via reflection).
seeds.question: Is there a logo on the BACK of the box?
seeds.answer: No
seeds.lever: Mirror shows reverse-image of FRONT through transparency? No: mirror shows back-of-box which has no logo; the XOB seen is mirror image of front logo. Confirm: back has no logo.

seeds.scene: Two photos of a stone sculpture from different viewpoints. From angle A (south side), 3 small carved figures are visible on the front. From angle B (north side), 5 small carved figures are visible on the back. Side view shows the sculpture has 4 sides with carved figures: front 3, back 5, left 2, right 1. Total = 11.
seeds.question: How many figures are TOTAL on the sculpture?
seeds.lever: Multi-view aggregation; sum each face's count.

seeds.scene: A photo of straight train tracks receding into the distance. The two parallel rails appear to converge at the horizon (vanishing point). A passenger on the train asks if the rails are actually converging.
seeds.question: Are the rails actually converging?
seeds.answer: No (parallel; convergence is a perspective illusion)
seeds.lever: Recognize linear perspective and the constant gauge of train tracks.

seeds.scene: A fisheye-lens photo of a basketball court. Straight lines on the court appear curved due to lens distortion. The center of the court is in the center of the photo (no distortion at center).
seeds.question: Are the actual court lines straight or curved?
seeds.answer: Straight (curvature is lens distortion)
seeds.lever: Recognize fisheye lens artifact.

seeds.scene: A drinking glass with water and a straw. Side view: straw appears to bend at the water surface (refraction). Top view: straw enters water at one point and exits at another, both visible from above without bending.
seeds.question: Is the straw actually bent?
seeds.answer: No (refraction makes it APPEAR bent)
seeds.lever: Reconcile two views; top view shows straight straw.

seeds.scene: Two views of the same room: an isometric (parallel projection) view and a one-point perspective view. In the isometric, the room dimensions are 4×3×3. In the perspective view, the back wall looks smaller due to depth.
seeds.question: What are the actual room dimensions?
seeds.answer: 4 × 3 × 3 (isometric is to-scale)
seeds.lever: Trust the isometric/orthographic measurement; reject perspective foreshortening.

seeds.scene: 10 axial MRI slices of a brain showing a tumor visible in slices 4, 5, 6, 7. The slice spacing is 5mm. Each slice tumor cross-section is approximately circular: slice 4 = 5mm diameter, slice 5 = 12mm, slice 6 = 12mm, slice 7 = 5mm.
seeds.question: Approximately what is the tumor's HEIGHT (along the slice axis)?
seeds.answer: Approximately 20 mm (4 slices × 5mm spacing)
seeds.lever: Aggregate slice count × spacing.

seeds.scene: An IKEA assembly instruction step shows the underside of a desktop with screw holes labeled. Step 4 says 'attach left leg here'. The instruction has a small icon showing the assembled view from above. Looking from above, the leg labelled 'left' is on the user's left when sitting at the desk.
seeds.question: When working with the desktop FACE-DOWN (underside up), the leg should be attached to the user's:
seeds.answer: right (because flipped face-down inverts left/right)
seeds.lever: Mental flip: face-down inverts horizontal orientation.

seeds.scene: Two security camera views of an indoor parking garage. Camera 1 covers the north half. Camera 2 covers the south half. There is a 3m overlap zone in the middle visible to both. Camera 1 sees 8 cars, Camera 2 sees 7 cars, the overlap shows 2 cars visible to both.
seeds.question: What is the TOTAL number of unique cars in the garage?
seeds.lever: Inclusion-exclusion: 8 + 7 - 2 = 13.

seeds.scene: Two photos of a dancer claimed to be in the same pose. Photo A taken from the front: arms raised in a 'V', left leg extended forward. Photo B from the side: arms raised in 'V' visible, but BOTH legs appear straight down — no extended leg.
seeds.question: Are the two photos showing the SAME pose?
seeds.answer: No (the leg extension is missing in photo B)
seeds.lever: Cross-view feature consistency check; identify the discrepancy.

seeds.scene: Two photos of an outdoor sculpture from different viewpoints, both taken at the same time. Photo 1: shadow of sculpture extends to the LEFT in the frame. Photo 2: shadow extends to the LEFT in the frame as well. The sun has not moved.
seeds.question: Are the two photos plausibly taken at the same time from different positions?
seeds.answer: No — shadows in photos from different viewpoints should appear in different directions in their respective frames if the sun is fixed
seeds.lever: Reasoning about shadow/sun geometry across viewpoints; same shadow direction in both frames implies same camera orientation, contradicting 'different viewpoints'.

seeds.scene: A standard 3-view engineering drawing of a single solid object: TOP view (an L-shape, 6×4 with a 2×2 notch removed at the top-right corner), FRONT view (rectangle 6 wide × 3 tall), SIDE view (rectangle 4 wide × 3 tall, with a hidden-line indicating a hole partially through). All in 1st-angle projection, with dimensions labeled. The L-shape clearly has equal-thickness in the top view.
seeds.question: What is the volume of the solid object?
seeds.answer: 60 cubic units
seeds.lever: Cross-correlate top (L-shape area = 6×4 − 2×2 = 20) × height from front view (= 3) → 60; ignore the 'hidden-line hole' which is partial and not subtracted in this question.

seeds.scene: Two flat mirrors stand vertically and meet along their common edge at a 60° angle (like an open book). A single small candle is placed exactly on the angle bisector, equidistant from both mirrors. The mirror system is photographed from above.
seeds.question: How many TOTAL candle images (excluding the actual physical candle) are visible to a viewer?
seeds.lever: Standard formula for two mirrors at angle θ: number of images = 360/θ − 1 = 360/60 − 1 = 5; not 6 (which would be common naive guess including the real candle).

seeds.domain: glass storefront door with painted text
seeds.scene: Two photographs of the SAME glass storefront door painted with the word 'CAFE' on the outside in solid red letters. Photo (a) is taken from the OUTSIDE looking in; the word reads correctly as 'CAFE'. Photo (b) is taken from INSIDE the cafe looking out; the word appears reversed (mirror-flipped horizontally).
seeds.question: When viewed from the inside, what does the four-letter word visually appear to spell out (writing the letter shapes left-to-right as seen)?
seeds.answer: EFAC
seeds.lever: Mirror flip: read the letters in reverse order, recognize that C, A, F, E individually flip but only F is visibly asymmetric; many models will incorrectly answer CAFE. The reversed left-to-right order is EFAC; some letters will look mirrored in shape.

seeds.scene: A standard analog wristwatch is shown reflected in a flat vertical mirror. In the mirrored image, the watch face shows hour hand pointing to '8' and minute hand pointing to '2' (i.e., 8:10 as it appears in the mirror).
seeds.question: What is the ACTUAL time on the watch?
seeds.lever: Mirror inverts horizontally; clock-face mirror trick: actual time = 12:00 − mirrored time = 12:00 − 8:10 = 3:50 (or equivalently subtract from 11:60). Common confusion: some say 4:50 or 8:10.

seeds.domain: asymmetric mug with handle and logo
seeds.scene: A coffee mug is shown in two photos: FRONT view (a logo 'Z' is centered on the visible side, no handle visible — hidden behind), SIDE view from the right (logo edge visible, handle visible on the right side, exiting toward the viewer's right). Inferred from these two: mug is opaque white; logo is on one face only.
seeds.question: If photographed from the BACK, would the logo be visible? Would the handle be on the viewer's LEFT or RIGHT?
seeds.answer: No logo visible; handle on viewer's LEFT.
seeds.lever: Spatial-rotation reasoning: front-view shows logo facing camera + handle behind; back-view rotates 180° → logo behind, handle now on viewer's left (mirror of front-view's right).

seeds.scene: An unrolled 360° panorama of a circular plaza, displayed as a wide horizontal strip. A statue is visible at the LEFT edge of the strip, AND ALSO at the RIGHT edge of the strip (because the panorama wraps around). Three other distinct landmarks (a clock tower, a fountain, a church) are visible at intermediate positions.
seeds.question: Counting unique physical landmarks (not duplicates from the panorama wraparound), how many landmarks are in the plaza?
seeds.lever: Statue appears twice (wraparound) but is one physical object; total = statue + tower + fountain + church = 4. Naive count gives 5.

seeds.scene: Two photos labeled L (left-eye) and R (right-eye) of the same scene with three balls labeled A, B, C. In the L image: A is at x=200px, B at x=350px, C at x=500px. In the R image: A at x=160px, B at x=320px, C at x=485px. (Each ball is shifted leftward in R relative to L by different amounts: A shifts 40, B shifts 30, C shifts 15.)
seeds.question: Which ball is FARTHEST from the camera?
seeds.answer: C
seeds.lever: Stereo disparity rule: larger disparity = closer. C has the smallest shift (15px) → farthest. Common error: ignore disparity and pick by visible size or position.

seeds.domain: asymmetric building photographed from two sides
seeds.scene: A two-story asymmetric building. Photo A taken from the NORTH side: a large blue door is visible on the LEFT half of the facade, a circular window on the RIGHT. A signpost in front says 'NORTH FACADE'. Photo B taken from the SOUTH side: a wooden double-door is visible on the LEFT half of THAT facade, and a square window on the RIGHT. The building has no floors with openings on east/west sides.
seeds.question: If you stand to the EAST of the building and look at it, the blue door (north facade) appears to which side of you: left or right?
seeds.answer: Right
seeds.lever: Mental rotation: looking east-to-west, north is on your right; the blue door (on the LEFT of the north facade as photographed) is on the side closer to the WEST end of the north wall. From an east-of-the-building viewer looking westward, the north wall is to your right; the door's left-of-north-facade position becomes the FAR end of the north wall. The door is on the right side (the north half of the building from your viewpoint).

seeds.scene: An unfolded cube net (cross shape: 4-square row + 1 above + 1 below the center square) drawn on grid paper. Each of the 6 faces has a distinct symbol: ★ ♦ ♣ ♥ ▲ ●. The diagram clearly shows the symbols on each face: leftmost = ★, then ♦ (left-of-center), then ♣ (center), ♥ (right-of-center), ● (rightmost), ▲ (above center).
seeds.question: When folded, which face is OPPOSITE to ♣?
seeds.answer: ● (the rightmost face)
seeds.lever: Cube-net opposite-face rule: in a 'plus'-shaped cross net, ★ and ● (the two extremes of the long arm) are opposite to one of the middle faces. Walking the net: ★ is two steps from ♣ → ★ folds to opposite of ♥; ● is two steps from ♣ → ● folds to opposite of ♣? Actually: ♣ is the BOTTOM (center of cross); ▲ above it folds to the TOP (opposite of ♣). Wait — re-examine: in the standard cross net the center square is the FRONT, and the top arm folds up to become TOP, bottom arm folds down to become BOTTOM, and the row endpoints fold to opposite each other. With ♣ as center (FRONT), ▲ is the TOP, then opposite of ♣ (FRONT) is BACK = ● (the far-right end of the row, which folds twice to become BACK). So opposite of ♣ = ●.

seeds.scene: A photo of a sunny park. A long tree shadow lies on the grass pointing TOWARD the bottom-right of the frame. A small compass icon overlaid in the corner points 'N' toward the top of the frame. Sun position is consistent with mid-afternoon in the northern hemisphere.
seeds.question: What time of day (approximately) was this photo taken?
seeds.answer: Mid-afternoon (sun in the western sky, shadow points east-northeast from the tree base; bottom-right of frame = south-east).
seeds.lever: Combine compass orientation (N up) + shadow direction (toward bottom-right = SE) → sun is in the NW; in the northern hemisphere this implies late morning or mid-afternoon depending on season — the most common answer matches mid-afternoon (sun west).

seeds.scene: In the display window, there are 5 croissants in the front layer, and the glass reflects the street scene; another 4 croissants in the back layer are visible through the gaps in the front layer.
seeds.question: How many croissants are there in total in the display window?
seeds.lever: Counting through the glass requires excluding reflection artifacts.

seeds.scene: A black-and-white striped straw is inserted into a glass beaker; it appears broken at the water surface, with the submerged part visually shifted to the right.
seeds.question: To which side does the submerged part of the straw visually shift?
seeds.answer: The right side
seeds.lever: Judging the displacement caused by refraction.

seeds.scene: Three translucent colored films are stacked: yellow covers blue to form a green area, while the red film only covers a corner of the blue film; the grid paper behind is visible through them.
seeds.question: Which overlapping area is green?
seeds.answer: The overlapping area between the yellow and blue films
seeds.lever: Translucent color overlay recognition.

seeds.scene: There are 3 real diamond rings in the display case; the glass top surface also reflects 3 virtual images; one of the real rings is almost aligned with its reflection.
seeds.question: How many real diamond rings are in the display case?
seeds.lever: Distinguishing between physical objects and mirror reflections.

seeds.scene: A number plate reading "27" is attached to the back wall of the water tank; when observed through the curved water surface, the last digit is slightly stretched, but the numbers remain legible.
seeds.question: What is the number on the back of the water tank?
seeds.lever: Text reading under water distortion.

seeds.scene: The shadows of the glass cup and the metal spoon partially overlap on the tabletop; the edges of the cup's shadow are soft and transparent, while the spoon's shadow is sharp and slender.
seeds.question: What object does the slender and sharp shadow come from?
seeds.answer: Metal spoon
seeds.lever: Distinguish the source of the shadow by its shape.

seeds.scene: Two angled mirrors cause the red hat to appear as a direct physical object, a primary reflection, and a secondary reflection; the secondary reflection is positioned further away.
seeds.question: How many real red hats are in the image?
seeds.lever: Suppression of counting multiple reflections.

seeds.scene: Two people stand behind a frosted glass door: one holds a long umbrella high up, and the other holds a square box; their silhouettes are blurry but their postures are clear.
seeds.question: Which person is holding the long umbrella?
seeds.answer: The person on the left
seeds.lever: Silhouette recognition under frosted obscuration.

seeds.scene: A small-text label "L8" is placed in front of a spherical glass dessert cup; when viewed through the center of the cup wall, the letters appear magnified, while the edge areas are stretched.
seeds.question: What is the code on the label?
seeds.answer: L8
seeds.lever: OCR under magnification and edge distortion by a spherical medium.

seeds.scene: Inside a transparent acrylic box, 2 model cars are arranged front to back; the front car blocks half of the rear car, and the box lid has a strong highlight.
seeds.question: How many model cars are there in total inside the box?
seeds.lever: Transparent container highlight + counting overlapping solid objects.

seeds.scene: A stage scene with a dancer wearing a costume that appears YELLOW under a normal white spotlight. The same dancer is now lit only by a BLUE spotlight (no white).
seeds.question: How does the costume appear under the blue spotlight?
seeds.answer: Black (or very dark)
seeds.lever: Yellow reflects red+green wavelengths, absorbs blue. Under pure blue light, no reflection → appears dark.

seeds.scene: Two photos of the same lake scene, one taken without polarized sunglasses (lots of glare on water surface, can't see fish below), one with polarized lens (no glare, fish clearly visible).
seeds.question: What does polarization remove?
seeds.answer: Reflected glare from horizontal water surface
seeds.lever: Polarization filters horizontally polarized reflected light.

seeds.scene: A magnifying glass held at varying distances above printed text. At distance d=2cm: text appears enlarged and upright. At d=15cm (focal length 10cm): text appears blurry. At d=25cm: text appears INVERTED and reduced.
seeds.question: Why does the text appear inverted at d=25cm?
seeds.answer: The lens is acting as a real-image projector when object is beyond focal length
seeds.lever: Convex lens: object inside f → virtual upright magnified; object outside f → real inverted image.

seeds.scene: A scene lit by TWO spotlights: one red and one green, illuminating a white wall with a person's body casting shadows. The body blocks one light at a time, creating overlapping shadows of different colors.
seeds.question: What colors are the two visible shadows on the wall?
seeds.answer: One green shadow (where the red light is blocked) and one red shadow (where the green light is blocked)
seeds.lever: Each shadow shows the color of the unblocked source: red blocked → green-only region (green shadow); green blocked → red-only region (red shadow).

seeds.scene: A double rainbow visible in the sky. The primary (brighter) rainbow has red on the OUTSIDE and violet on the INSIDE. The secondary (fainter) rainbow above it has the colors REVERSED. The rainbow appears in the eastern sky.
seeds.question: Which direction is the sun?
seeds.answer: West (behind the observer)
seeds.lever: Rainbow forms on the side of sky opposite the sun, antisolar point in middle of bow arc.

seeds.scene: A prism splits a beam of white light into a rainbow. The colors emerging are bent at different angles. The red emerges with the LEAST bending, violet with the MOST bending.
seeds.question: What color appears at the TOP of the spectrum (closest to undeflected beam direction)?
seeds.answer: Red
seeds.lever: Red has longest wavelength → least refraction → closest to original beam direction.

seeds.scene: A glow-in-the-dark toy seen in two states: just removed from sunlight (glows brightly green), and after 4 hours in darkness (glows very faintly).
seeds.question: What process is responsible for the change?
seeds.answer: Phosphorescence decay (released energy diminishes over time)
seeds.lever: Identify phosphorescence physics.

seeds.scene: A concave shaving mirror with focal length 20 cm. Object distance: 10 cm (inside focal length). The image appears enlarged and upright.
seeds.question: Is the image REAL or VIRTUAL?
seeds.answer: Virtual
seeds.lever: Concave mirror with object inside focal length → virtual upright magnified image.

seeds.scene: A soap film viewed in white light shows swirling rainbow colors that change with the film thickness. Thinner regions appear black (destructive interference), thicker regions show various colors.
seeds.question: What physical phenomenon causes the colors?
seeds.answer: Thin-film interference
seeds.lever: Identify thin-film interference physics.

seeds.scene: Two photos: same dollar bill under normal light (no special markings visible), and under UV blacklight (a hidden security strip glows bright blue).
seeds.question: What property does the security strip have?
seeds.answer: Fluorescence (absorbs UV, emits visible light)
seeds.lever: UV → visible emission = fluorescence.

seeds.scene: A photo through a cheap telescope shows the moon with purple and red color fringes around its edges, especially at the limb.
seeds.question: What is causing the color fringes?
seeds.answer: Chromatic aberration (different wavelengths focus at different distances)
seeds.lever: Identify chromatic aberration.

seeds.scene: A photo of the view through a 3-mirror kaleidoscope. The original chamber has 4 colored beads. The image shows a 6-fold symmetric pattern with the beads multiplied.
seeds.question: How many bead images are visible in the symmetric pattern?
seeds.answer: 24 (4 beads × 6-fold symmetry)
seeds.lever: Multiply original elements by symmetry order.

seeds.scene: A photo of a computer monitor displayed on a TV screen, viewed from a phone camera. A moiré interference pattern of curves appears on the captured image, despite neither screen having such curves on display.
seeds.question: Why does the moiré pattern appear?
seeds.answer: Pixel-grid alignment mismatch creates beat-frequency interference between the two regular grids
seeds.lever: Identify moiré as interference between two regular periodic patterns.

seeds.scene: An Ishihara color-blind test plate with red dots arranged to spell '74' inside a field of green dots. A person with red-green color blindness sees uniform color (no number visible).
seeds.question: What does a color-blind person see?
seeds.answer: Uniform dots / no discernible number
seeds.lever: Color-blindness physiology; collapses red-green discrimination.

seeds.scene: A frosted glass shower door with a person standing 5 cm behind. The silhouette is sharp. Same door with person 50 cm behind: silhouette becomes blurry and lighter.
seeds.question: Why does distance affect the visibility of the silhouette?
seeds.answer: Frosted glass scatters light; greater object-glass distance increases light spreading before reaching glass
seeds.lever: Scattering depth physics with frosted glass.

seeds.scene: Two polarizing filters held in front of a light source. When their polarization axes are aligned (parallel), maximum light passes. When rotated 90° (crossed), no light passes (black). At 45°, intermediate brightness.
seeds.question: What law describes this behavior?
seeds.answer: Malus's law: I = I₀·cos²(θ)
seeds.lever: Identify Malus's law for crossed polarizers.

seeds.scene: Two identical orange circles. Circle A is surrounded by a ring of LARGE blue circles. Circle B is surrounded by SMALL blue circles. The center circles appear to be different sizes (B looks larger than A despite being identical).
seeds.question: Are the orange circles ACTUALLY the same size?
seeds.answer: Yes (Ebbinghaus illusion)
seeds.lever: Recognize the visual illusion; measure independently.

seeds.scene: A lenticular print card showing two different images depending on viewing angle: from the left, a smiling face; from the right, a frowning face.
seeds.question: What technology produces this effect?
seeds.answer: Lenticular lenses (parallel ridges of plastic each acting as a tiny prism/lens)
seeds.lever: Identify lenticular printing technology.

seeds.scene: A photo of a Morpho butterfly with brilliant blue iridescent wings. The blue is not from pigment; the wings under a microscope show layered nano-structures.
seeds.question: What physical phenomenon creates the blue color?
seeds.answer: Structural coloration via thin-film interference / photonic crystal
seeds.lever: Distinguish structural color from pigment-based color.

seeds.scene: Inside a fish tank, a fish looking upward at the water surface sees its own reflection on the underside of the surface. From a steep angle, the surface looks like a mirror; from straight up, the sky is visible (refracted).
seeds.question: What angle marks the boundary (Snell's window edge)?
seeds.answer: About 48.6° from vertical (the critical angle for water-air = arcsin(1/1.33))
seeds.lever: Total internal reflection critical angle for water.

seeds.scene: A stage with a yellow shirt illuminated by a magenta spotlight (red+blue light, no green).
seeds.question: How does the yellow shirt appear under the magenta light?
seeds.answer: red (yellow reflects red and green; only red is in the light)
seeds.lever: Subtractive reflection × additive light: yellow pigment passes red+green; magenta light has red+blue → only red survives.

seeds.scene: Two side-by-side photos of a pond surface; left without polarizer (heavy surface glare hides fish), right with polarizer (clear view of fish below).
seeds.question: What does the polarizer remove?
seeds.answer: specular surface reflections (glare)
seeds.lever: Recognize that polarizing filters reduce specular reflection from non-metallic surfaces.

seeds.scene: A magnifying glass at distance d=25cm above a printed page; text appears inverted and reduced in the lens, where focal length is 10cm.
seeds.question: Why does the text appear inverted at d=25cm?
seeds.answer: object is beyond 2f (focal length 10cm), so a real inverted reduced image forms
seeds.lever: Apply thin-lens imaging behavior: object > 2f → real, inverted, smaller image.

seeds.scene: A sky photo with the sun visible behind the camera at low angle; a rainbow arc visible in front in the spray of a fountain.
seeds.question: Where must the sun be relative to the photographer for this rainbow geometry?
seeds.answer: behind the photographer (at 0° azimuth from view direction)
seeds.lever: Apply rainbow geometry: anti-solar point is at observer's shadow direction.

seeds.scene: A glass half-filled with water; a pencil rests in it; the pencil appears bent at the air-water interface.
seeds.question: Why does the submerged portion of the pencil appear shifted?
seeds.answer: refraction at the air-water boundary (water has higher refractive index)
seeds.lever: Recognize Snell's-law bending of light at interface.

seeds.scene: A frosted glass cube held above a white surface; the shadow shows a soft penumbra and the central area is gray rather than fully dark.
seeds.question: Why is the shadow not fully dark?
seeds.answer: translucent material transmits diffuse light through it
seeds.lever: Distinguish transmittance vs opacity in shadow formation.

seeds.scene: A person standing facing a flat vertical mirror; they raise their left hand.
seeds.question: Which hand of the mirror image is raised, from the viewer's perspective?
seeds.answer: the hand on the viewer's right side of the mirror image
seeds.lever: Mirror reverses front-back, not literally L-R; reasoning about mirror parity.

seeds.scene: An outdoor portrait with a circular lens flare arc across the upper-right of the frame.
seeds.question: Roughly where is the sun in this scene?
seeds.answer: outside the frame, opposite the flare direction (lower-left of camera)
seeds.lever: Lens flares appear opposite the actual light source through the optical axis.

seeds.scene: A photo of a CD reflecting white light, showing rainbow color bands radiating from the center.
seeds.question: Why does the CD display rainbow colors?
seeds.answer: diffraction from the regularly-spaced track grooves separates wavelengths
seeds.lever: Recognize diffraction grating effect from periodic surface structure.

seeds.scene: A scene with two colored stage lights (red and green) hitting a white wall; an object between them casts two shadows on the wall: where red is blocked, the shadow appears green; where green is blocked, the shadow appears red.
seeds.question: Why do the colored shadows appear?
seeds.answer: each shadow blocks one color, allowing only the other color's light to illuminate that region
seeds.lever: Reason about color light sources and shadow as light-source occlusion.

seeds.scene: A puddle with a thin oil film showing iridescent rainbow colors that shift as viewing angle changes.
seeds.question: What causes the changing colors?
seeds.answer: thin-film interference; color depends on film thickness and viewing angle
seeds.lever: Recognize thin-film interference as cause of iridescence.

seeds.scene: A long-distance highway photo with a shimmering 'wet' patch on the road far ahead, reflecting sky.
seeds.question: What causes the apparent water on the road?
seeds.answer: inferior mirage from light refracting through hot-air layer above the asphalt
seeds.lever: Recognize hot-air refraction as cause of inferior mirage.

seeds.scene: A concave shaving mirror with an object placed beyond its focal point; a real, inverted image forms in space in front of it.
seeds.question: Where can a card be placed to display this image?
seeds.answer: between the mirror and the object, at the image distance
seeds.lever: Apply mirror equation to locate real-image plane.

seeds.scene: Two identically-shaped balls under the same light: one polished chrome (sharp environment reflection visible on surface), one matte white (smooth shading, no environment image).
seeds.question: Which surface is specular?
seeds.answer: the chrome ball
seeds.lever: Distinguish reflection types by sharpness of mirrored environment.

seeds.scene: A fish viewed through the side wall of a glass aquarium appears larger than its actual size.

seeds.domain: prism dispersing white light onto screen
seeds.scene: A glass triangular prism on an optical bench. White light from a source hits the prism's face; the prism disperses the light into a spectrum on a screen. The spectrum from RED (deviated LEAST) to VIOLET (deviated MOST) is clearly visible, with colors sorted by bending angle.
seeds.question: Which color of light is deviated the LEAST by the prism, and why?
seeds.answer: Red light is deviated the least because red light has the lowest refractive index in glass (n is smallest for red). Violet has the highest refractive index, so it is deviated the most.
seeds.lever: VLM sees 'rainbow from prism' and may confuse 'violet is most bent' with 'violet is most visible' or may invert the order. T requires mapping refractive index to bending angle: n_red < n_violet → θ_red < θ_violet.

seeds.scene: A laboratory optical bench with a light source, Polarizer 1 (vertical axis), Polarizer 2 (rotated 45° from Polarizer 1), and an intensity detector. Unpolarized light of intensity I₀ enters Polarizer 1, exits Polarizer 2, and is measured.

seeds.answer: I₀/4 (or 0.25 I₀). After P1: I₀/2 (unpolarized → linear). After P2 at 45°: (I₀/2) cos²(45°) = (I₀/2)(1/2) = I₀/4.
seeds.lever: VLM may predict 'two polarizers at 45° transmit something' without quantifying. T requires combining unpolarized-to-polarized halving with Malus's law: cos²(45°) = 1/2.

seeds.domain: optical fiber with labeled critical angle
seeds.scene: A schematic of a glass fiber (n=1.5) surrounded by air (n=1.0). Several light rays are shown inside the fiber striking the side boundary at different incident angles: ray A at 30° (refracts and escapes), ray B at 40° (mostly reflects), ray C at 50° (totally internally reflected, bounces back). A label indicates the critical angle region.
seeds.question: What is the critical angle for total internal reflection at a glass-air interface (n_glass=1.5, n_air=1.0)?
seeds.answer: θ_c ≈ 41.8°. sin(θ_c) = n_air/n_glass = 1.0/1.5 → θ_c = arcsin(2/3) ≈ 41.8°. Rays at angles > 41.8° are totally internally reflected.
seeds.lever: VLM sees 'light in fiber' and may answer 'all light is trapped' (S, generic understanding) without deriving the critical angle. T requires applying sin(θ_c) = n₂/n₁ and computing arcsin.

seeds.scene: A schematic of three meshed gears in a row. Gear A on the left has 12 teeth and rotates at 60 rpm clockwise. Gear B in the middle has 24 teeth, meshed with A. Gear C on the right has 36 teeth, meshed with B. Tooth counts and the rotation arrow on A are labeled.
seeds.question: At what rpm and in which direction does Gear C rotate?
seeds.answer: 20 rpm clockwise
seeds.lever: Gear ratio: 60 × 12/24 × 24/36 = 60 × 12/36 = 20 rpm; direction flips with each mesh (CW → CCW → CW).

seeds.scene: A block-and-tackle pulley system: a single load is supported by 4 rope segments going over a fixed top pulley and around two movable bottom pulleys. The free end of the rope is pulled downward.
seeds.question: What force is needed at the free end to lift a 200 N load (assuming ideal/frictionless pulleys)?
seeds.lever: MA = number of supporting rope segments = 4; F = load/MA = 200/4 = 50 N.

seeds.scene: A Rube-Goldberg-style diagram. Step 1: a marble released at the top of a ramp. Step 2: marble strikes a domino, knocking down a row of dominoes. Step 3: the last domino tips a small lever. Step 4: the lever releases a string holding a basket. Step 5: the basket falls onto a switch. Step 6: the switch turns on a fan. Step 7: the fan blows a paper boat across water. Step 8: the boat hits a button that rings a bell.
seeds.question: How many distinct mechanical interactions occur from marble release to bell ring?
seeds.answer: 8 (or 7 transitions between stages 1→8)
seeds.lever: Counting causal links in a long chain; tests sequential reasoning.

seeds.scene: A horizontal seesaw balanced on a triangular fulcrum. On the left arm, 60 cm from the fulcrum, sits a 5 kg block. On the right arm, at distance d from the fulcrum, sits a 3 kg block. The seesaw is in static equilibrium.
seeds.question: What is d?
seeds.answer: 100 cm (1 meter)
seeds.lever: Torque balance: 5 × 60 = 3 × d → d = 100 cm.

seeds.scene: A row of standing dominoes spaced 4 cm apart. Each domino is 6 cm tall and 1 cm wide. The first domino is being pushed slightly (will tip). At position 7, however, there is a gap of 12 cm before the next domino.
seeds.question: Will the chain reaction reach the last domino past the 12 cm gap?
seeds.answer: No — a 6 cm tall domino can only push a neighbor that is within roughly its own height; a 12 cm gap exceeds the tipping range, so the chain stops at domino 7
seeds.lever: Physical reasoning about domino spacing vs height.

seeds.scene: A simple schematic showing a 9V battery, a switch, a resistor (100 Ω), and a small light bulb in series. The switch is drawn in the OPEN position.
seeds.question: Is the bulb lit?
seeds.answer: No — the open switch breaks the circuit, no current flows
seeds.lever: Reading switch state in a schematic and inferring downstream consequence.

seeds.scene: A circuit with a 12V battery and three resistors: R1 = 4 Ω in series with the parallel combination of R2 = 6 Ω and R3 = 12 Ω. All values labeled.
seeds.question: What is the total current drawn from the battery?

seeds.scene: A single fixed pulley at the top of a frame. A rope passes over it. The right end of the rope is attached to a bucket on the ground. A person grasps the left end and pulls downward.
seeds.question: When the person pulls down on the left end, which direction does the bucket move?
seeds.answer: Up
seeds.lever: Direction reasoning for a fixed pulley (force redirection).

seeds.scene: A wooden block of mass 2 kg sits on a wooden ramp inclined at 25°. The coefficient of static friction between block and ramp is given as μs = 0.3.
seeds.question: Does the block slide down the ramp on its own?
seeds.answer: Yes — tan(25°) ≈ 0.466 > μs = 0.3, so gravitational component along the ramp exceeds maximum static friction; the block slides
seeds.lever: Compare tan(angle) vs coefficient of friction.

seeds.scene: A hydraulic press: small piston of area 5 cm² connected to large piston of area 100 cm² via incompressible fluid. A 10 N force is applied downward on the small piston.
seeds.question: What is the maximum lifting force at the large piston (assuming ideal conditions)?
seeds.lever: Pascal's principle: F2 = F1 × (A2/A1) = 10 × 100/5 = 200 N.

seeds.scene: Two simple pendulums hung side by side. Pendulum A has length 1 m. Pendulum B has length 4 m. Both released simultaneously from the same small angle.
seeds.question: Which pendulum has the longer period, and by what factor?
seeds.answer: Pendulum B; its period is twice as long (T ∝ √L; √4 = 2)
seeds.lever: Pendulum period scaling with √L.

seeds.scene: Three rows of dominoes arranged in a Y-shape. The trunk has 5 dominoes leading to a junction. From the junction, two branches each have 4 dominoes. The first domino in the trunk is tipped. All spacings allow tipping to propagate.
seeds.question: How many dominoes will fall in total?
seeds.answer: 13 (5 trunk + 4 + 4 branches)
seeds.lever: Counting cascade in a branched chain.

seeds.scene: A wheel-and-axle system: wheel radius 30 cm, axle radius 5 cm. A rope around the wheel is pulled by a person with force F. A load hangs from a rope around the axle.
seeds.question: If the person pulls with 20 N on the wheel rope, what load can be lifted (ideal conditions)?

seeds.scene: A circuit with a battery, a bulb, and two switches in PARALLEL with each other (both in line with the bulb but in alternate paths). Switch S1 is closed; switch S2 is open.
seeds.question: Is the bulb lit?
seeds.answer: Yes — current can flow through closed S1; the parallel arrangement means either switch alone is sufficient
seeds.lever: Parallel switch logic (OR-gate behavior).

seeds.scene: Same as previous but the two switches are now in SERIES. S1 closed, S2 open.
seeds.question: Is the bulb lit?
seeds.answer: No — series switches act as AND; S2 open breaks the circuit
seeds.lever: Series switch logic (AND-gate behavior).

seeds.scene: Two parallel tracks from the same starting height to the same ending height. Track A is straight and slopes uniformly down. Track B has a dip in the middle (it goes down further, then climbs back up to the same end height as A). Two identical balls released simultaneously, one on each track. Both ramps are smooth (frictionless).
seeds.question: Which ball reaches the end first?
seeds.answer: Ball B (the dipped track) — it accelerates to a higher speed in the dip, completing the journey faster despite the longer path; classic 'brachistochrone-like' result
seeds.lever: Counter-intuitive physics: dipped track is faster despite longer path.

seeds.scene: A helium-filled balloon tied to a small basket holding 50 g of cargo. The system is in static equilibrium hovering in mid-air at room temperature and pressure. Helium density 0.18 g/L; air density 1.2 g/L; balloon-fabric mass 5 g.
seeds.question: What approximate volume of helium is the balloon holding (ignoring basket and string mass)?
seeds.answer: Approximately 53.9 L (≈54 L). For lift balance: V × (1.2 - 0.18) g/L = 55 g → V = 55/1.02 ≈ 53.9 L
seeds.lever: Buoyancy force balance with displaced air.

seeds.scene: A ball on a rope (length 1 m) is held horizontal and released, swinging down to strike a stationary ball on a frictionless surface at the bottom of the swing. Both balls are identical mass; collision is perfectly elastic.
seeds.question: After the collision, what happens to each ball?
seeds.answer: The swinging ball stops; the stationary ball moves off horizontally with the velocity the swinging ball had at the bottom (Newton's cradle behavior for equal masses, elastic collision)
seeds.lever: Elastic collision between equal masses transfers all velocity.

seeds.scene: Two open containers of water connected by a thin flexible tube. Container A is on a high shelf with water level 80 cm above the floor. Container B is on the floor with water level 10 cm above the floor. The tube is filled with water and forms an inverted-U siphon.
seeds.question: Which way does water flow through the siphon?
seeds.answer: From Container A to Container B (high to low water level)
seeds.lever: Siphon physics — flow follows the head difference.

seeds.scene: A compound-lever diagram. Lever 1 is a class-1 lever with a 2 m long arm divided 1:1 about the fulcrum (effort arm = load arm = 1 m). Lever 1's right end pushes down on the left end of Lever 2, which is also class-1 with a 1 m arm divided so that the effort arm (the side being pushed by Lever 1) is 75 cm and the load arm is 25 cm. A 10 N force is applied to the left end of Lever 1.
seeds.question: What force is exerted at the load end of Lever 2 (ideal conditions)?
seeds.lever: Compound MA: Lever 1 transmits 10 N (1:1 arms); Lever 2 multiplies by effort/load arm ratio 75/25 = 3, giving 30 N.

seeds.scene: A lit candle is placed under a closed glass jar, sealed at the bottom by a non-porous tray.
seeds.question: What will happen to the candle flame after a few seconds?
seeds.answer: The flame will extinguish once the oxygen inside the jar is consumed
seeds.lever: Combustion requires oxygen; closed system depletes it.

seeds.scene: A tall glass partly filled with water. A large ice cube floats in it; the water level reaches a marked line. The ice gradually melts.
seeds.question: After the ice fully melts, how does the water level compare to the marked line?
seeds.answer: The water level remains at the same marked line
seeds.lever: Classic counter-intuitive result: melted ice fills exactly the displaced volume.

seeds.scene: A ball rolls off the end of a horizontal table at velocity 3 m/s. The table is 1.25 m above the floor. Air resistance negligible.
seeds.question: How far horizontally does the ball travel before hitting the floor?
seeds.answer: Approximately 1.5 m (time to fall: t = √(2h/g) = √(2.5/9.8) ≈ 0.5 s; distance = 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 m)
seeds.lever: Projectile motion decomposition.

seeds.scene: A scissor-jack diagram. Turning the handle 1 full rotation (360°) advances the screw 2 mm. The screw separates two diagonal bars whose vertical-to-horizontal motion ratio at the current position is 4:1 (vertical lift gain). The handle's effective lever arm is 200 mm.
seeds.question: How much vertical lift results from one full handle rotation?
seeds.answer: 8 mm (2 mm screw advance × 4 lift ratio)
seeds.lever: Combining screw thread pitch with mechanical-advantage geometry.

seeds.scene: A diagram of a double pendulum: one rigid rod hung from a pivot, with a second rod connected at the lower end of the first via a free joint. Both rods are released from a high horizontal position simultaneously.
seeds.question: Is the long-term motion of the second mass deterministic and predictable from the initial conditions?
seeds.answer: Mathematically deterministic but exhibits chaotic behavior — small initial-condition differences lead to large divergence over time, making it practically unpredictable beyond a short window
seeds.lever: Chaotic systems' sensitivity to initial conditions.

seeds.scene: A rope wrapped 2 full turns around a vertical pole. One end of the rope holds a hanging weight of 100 kg. The other end is held by a person.
seeds.question: Approximately, with what minimal hand force can the person hold the 100 kg weight given a friction coefficient between rope and pole of 0.3?
seeds.answer: Approximately 2.3 kg-force (≈22 N). Capstan equation: T_load/T_hold = e^(μθ) = e^(0.3 × 4π) ≈ e^3.77 ≈ 43. So T_hold ≈ 100/43 ≈ 2.3 kg-force
seeds.lever: Capstan / belt-friction equation; non-obvious massive amplification.

seeds.scene: A standard Newton's cradle with 5 identical steel balls suspended in a row. Three balls on the left are pulled back and released together to strike the remaining 2 stationary balls.
seeds.question: After the impact, what happens?
seeds.answer: Three balls swing out on the right side at the same speed and angle as the released three; the two leftmost balls remain (with the middle one in the original line briefly stationary, then swinging back)
seeds.lever: Conservation of momentum and energy in a Newton's cradle with N released ≠ N stationary.

seeds.scene: A hanging mobile diagram. Top crossbar pivots at center; left side of bar (length 30 cm) holds a single 4 kg object. Right side (length L cm) holds a smaller crossbar from which two 1 kg objects hang at distances 5 cm and 10 cm from that smaller bar's pivot. The smaller bar is itself in equilibrium.
seeds.question: What is L for the top bar to balance?
seeds.answer: 60 cm — total weight on right = 2 kg; torque balance: 4 × 30 = 2 × L → L = 60 cm. (The smaller bar's internal balance is ensured separately.)
seeds.lever: Hierarchical torque balance in a compound mobile.

seeds.scene: A circuit with a battery, a bulb, and a wire that bypasses (short-circuits) the bulb directly from one terminal of the bulb to the other. The wire has near-zero resistance compared to the bulb.
seeds.question: Is the bulb lit?
seeds.answer: No — current preferentially flows through the near-zero-resistance shorting wire, bypassing the bulb
